"Here we have one of the quietest and most flexible cars on the market, capable of whispering along in top gear at 10mph or leaping into its 150mph stride on the brief depression of a pedal. A practical touring car, this, with its wide doors and capacious luggage space, yet it has a sheer beauty of line which easily beats the Italians at their own particular game."

There have been few better summaries of the Jaguar E-Type's manifest virtues than John Bolster's, penned for Autosport shortly after the car's debut in 1961. Introduced in 3.8-litre form, the E-Type caused a sensation when it appeared, with instantly classic lines and a 150mph (241km/h) top speed. The newcomer's design owed much to that of the racing D-Type: a monocoque tub forming the main structure while a tubular spaceframe extended forwards to support the engine. The latter was the same 3.8-litre, triple-carburettor 'S' unit first offered as an option on the preceding XK150. An optimistic 265bhp was claimed, but whatever the installed horsepower, the E-Type's performance did not disappoint; firstly, because it weighed around 500lb (227kg) less than the XK150 and secondly because aerodynamicist Malcolm Sayer used experience gained with the D-Type to create one of the most elegant and efficient shapes ever to grace a motor car. Indeed, even Enzo Ferrari was forced to concede that the E-Type was 'the most beautiful car ever made'.

Taller drivers though, could find the interior somewhat lacking in space, a criticism addressed by the introduction of foot wells (and other, more minor, modifications) early in 1962. But of all the versions of Jaguar's long-lived and much-loved sports car, it is the very early 'flat floor' 3.8-litre cars built prior to February 1962, which, for many enthusiasts, remain the most desirable. 

According to its accompanying Jaguar Heritage Production Record Trace Certificate, this particular example - chassis number '876192' - was built on 23rd November 1961 and despatched to Jaguar Cars' New York distributor eight days later. Originally finished in Carmen Red with black leather and matching hood (the same as today), it was supplied new by Falvey Motors of Ferndale, Michigan to a W H Mansfield. Relocated to the more car-friendly Californian climate thereafter, the E-Type was repatriated to the UK by the immediately preceding owner during late 2014 on the understanding that it was 'rust free' and retained 'all factory sheet metal, no cut out or replacement panels'. Said to be a 'nice driver' at the time, the E-Type was nevertheless entrusted to renowned marque specialist XK Engineering of Coventry with instructions that they restore the car to its former glory. 

Stripped back to bare metal and re-profiled as necessary, the bodywork was then painstakingly re-sprayed in its original Carmen Red, while the interior was re-trimmed in black, likewise to factory specification. The wiring, fuel system, exhaust, brakes, steering, and suspension all received attention, with numerous components being refurbished and repainted. The brightwork was renewed or re-plated, and a brand new black hood installed. Considerable time and effort was spent on ensuring that the opening panels (bonnet, boot, doors) fitted properly and sat well within their apertures. Rubber seals were replaced throughout and the wire wheels shod with fresh Avon tyres. In keeping with XK Engineering's ethos, the wood-rim steering wheel was refurbished rather than replaced because it was deemed to be the one with which the car had left Brown's Lane. Crucially retaining its original 'matching numbers' engine, this E-Type has been upgraded with one of Getrag's five-speed manual gearboxes. 

Our vendor purchased the E-Type from Bonhams' sale at the Goodwood Revival Meeting in September 2018 (Lot 276). Since then, the car has seen little use while being properly maintained and stored in a heated garage. The E-Type is currently registered in the Netherlands and has Dutch registration papers. A testament to XK Engineering's peerless craftsmanship, it remains worthy of the closest inspection.

 "Let's just go straight to it: the Ferrari F355 is one of the best cars ever to have come out of Maranello. The 355 replaced the rather lacklustre 348 and was a distinct improvement in both looks and dynamic ability. A quantum leap, if you like." â Auto Express. 

First presented to the motoring press in May 1994, the F355 effectively reforged the reputation of Ferrari's V8 which, 328 and 348 notwithstanding, had suffered since the introduction of the Mondial 'world car'. The latter, with its four seats, well-appointed interior, and - relatively - soft ride, was considered far too sensible to be a 'proper' Ferrari; the F355 though, was cast in the mould of that great drivers' car, the Dino 246GT. Just how great an advance it was may be gauged from the fact that the F355's best time around Ferrari's Fiorano test track was three seconds quicker than the formidable 512TR's. 

Despite its prodigious performance the F355 was no mere 'racer on the road', but a thoroughly modern automobile employing state-of-the-art technology, in the form of computer-controlled variable damping, to reconcile the differing requirements of ultimate roadholding and acceptable comfort. A light-action clutch, proportional power-assisted steering, and driver's air bag were other features calculated to make the car reassuringly user-friendly. 

The heart of the F355, though, was its phenomenal 3.5-litre V8 engine. Equipped with four overhead camshafts and five valves per cylinder - a layout borrowed from Ferrari's Formula 1 engine - this remarkable unit produced a claimed 370bhp at 8,250rpm, with 268lb/ft of torque available from 5,000 to 6,500rpm. A six-speed manual gearbox, mounted transversely behind the longitudinally disposed engine, ensured a sufficiency of ratios to keep the motor on the boil whatever the situation. Subsequently the F355 could be ordered with the Formula 1-developed six-speed automated manual transmission. 

Delivered new to its first lady owner in Hamburg via the local Ferrari concessionaire Satzer Granturismo on 14th August 1997, this stunning F355 with the desirable six-speed manual gearbox is finished in the attractive and rare colour combination of Giallo Fly with a black leather interior. The original service book lists six services at 4,785 km, 18,510, 28,130, 38,477 and 43,341 km. More recently the car was treated to a comprehensive engine-out service which included the fitment of new timing belts etc. and was executed by Ferrari specialist EDCO (Eddy Colanbeen) in Gent/Belgium on 17th April 2025. A detailed invoice with pictures for â¬ 7,695.98 is on file. 

This strikingly beautiful Ferrari V8 is offered with German registration documents, the original service book, aforementioned invoice and an owner's manual.

'Exclusive' is a much bandied-about word in the classic car world, but it is a most apt description of the Mercedes-Benz 280 SE 3.5. Why? Because at $13,500 in 1970 its price was not only $3,500 more than that of the equivalent Mercedes-Benz saloon but also more than double that of a Cadillac Deville CoupÃ©! Commonplace it was not. 

The 3.5-litre version of the 280 SE typifies the resurgence of larger-engined Mercedes-Benz models that began in the late 1960s and early 1970s, when the progressive easing of fiscal constraints, which had dissuaded customers from buying cars with large capacity engines, encouraged the German manufacturer to offer bigger, more potent power units. Thus, the ultra-luxurious 280 SE CoupÃ©/Cabriolet and 300 SEL saloon were the models chosen by Mercedes-Benz to launch its magnificent new 3.5-litre V8 engine in September 1969. An over-square design featuring a cast-iron block and aluminium-alloy cylinder heads, each equipped with a single overhead camshaft, this all-new, state-of-the-art power unit produced 200bhp courtesy of Bosch electronic fuel injection and transistorized ignition. 

The new V8 engine had particularly smooth-running characteristics and endowed the 280 SE 3.5 with performance superior to that of many out-and-out sports cars. Thus equipped, the CoupÃ©/Cabriolet was good for 125mph (200km/h) with 60mph (97km/h) reachable in 9.5 seconds, a substantial improvement on the six-cylinder version's figures. As befitted top-of-the-range luxury models, the 280 SE 3.5 CoupÃ© and Cabriolet came equipped with automatic transmission, power windows, and a stereo radio as standard. 

Although the equivalent SEL saloon used the 'New Generation' bodyshell, the 280 SE CoupÃ© and Cabriolet kept the elegant coachwork that had debuted back in 1960/1961 on the 220 SE. Nevertheless, there had been some refinements made: the radiator shell was lower and wider, with a correspondingly flatter front end to the bonnet, a characteristic that has led to enthusiasts referring to these face-lifted cars as 'flat radiator' models, while the bumpers were now fitted with rubber strips. Significantly, the 280 SE 3.5 was to be the final model featuring this long-established and much-admired body style. It was truly Mercedes-Benz's flagship model, representing status, luxury, and reliability. Only 1,232 Cabriolets were built, and today these last-of-the-line classics are highly sought after by discerning Mercedes-Benz collectors. 

The original order for this 280 SE 3.5 Cabriolet was completed by the Mercedes-Benz factory on 24th April 1970, and the car was delivered to Wuppertal, West Germany for first registration. It is number 1,128 of the 1,232 V8 Cabriolets and was built towards the end of the W111 Series production. The car was ordered in white (DB050) with red (243) leather, black mohair convertible top, central shift automatic transmission, and with the factory options of a rear fog light, locking glove compartment, ivory coloured steering wheel, front and side windowpanes (heat-absorbing glass) and combined European taillights. Later additions include Behr air conditioning, seat belts, and a passenger-side door mirror.

In 1993, the car was purchased by the current owner and registered in Paris. Since this time, it was predominantly used on the Continent for 24 years before being imported and registered in the UK. During 2017 a sympathetic restoration was carried out retaining all of the car's original colours and features, while that same year an hydraulic power cabriolet roof conversion was installed (with manual front unlock). Regularly maintained and stored for the last two years, the car runs and drives but will need fully checking over before returning to the road. "Jochen Neerpasch was the man who was responsible for the birth of BMW's only production supercar. BMW's audacious Motorsport manager wanted a car to take over the racing mantle of the highly successful CSL, to create a car which could do battle with Porsche in the World Sports Car Championship and could win at Le Mans. Unlike the CSL, its successor would not be a front-engined car, but a radically different machine: it evolved as the mid-engined M1." - Chris Rees, BMW M-Series.

A proposed Group 5 'Silhouette Formula' for production-based cars triggered the M1 programme in the mid-1970s, the basis being a mid-engined concept car designed in-house at BMW by Paul Bracq. Head of BMW's newly formed Motorsport Division, former racing driver Jochen Neerpasch was responsible for masterminding this ambitious project, whose aims included taking on rivals Porsche in the World Sports Car Championship and, ultimately, victory at Le Mans. 

M1 development was contracted first to Lamborghini and then to Giorgetto Giugiaro's Ital Design, although almost all cars ended up being built by coachbuilders Baur in Germany. Giugiaro's compact coupÃ© bodywork in glassfibre was wrapped around a multi-tubular spaceframe chassis, while a twin-overhead-cam, four-valves-per-cylinder version of BMW's 3.5-litre inline six, driving via a ZF five-speed transaxle, provided the motive power. 

The M1's wedge-shaped coachwork proved highly efficient aerodynamically, needing very little in the way of additional spoilers and wings in race configuration. Lamborghini's Gianpaolo Dallara had been responsible for developing the suspension, which followed racing practice by using unequal-length wishbones at front and rear. Soberly trimmed in black and grey, the M1's interior was exceptionally well equipped for a sports car, much of it sourced from the luxurious 6 Series. Notable featured included Recaro seats, air conditioning, electric windows, remotely operated door mirrors and a heated rear screen. 

First shown at the Paris Motor Show in 1978, the road-going version came with 273bhp and a claimed top speed of 161mph (260km/h), while Autocar magazine managed to clock a highly respectable 0-60mph (0-96km/h) time of 5.5 seconds. Writing in Autocar and quoted by Chris Rees, racing driver John Miles commented that the M1 was "a beautifully responsive and sometimes thrilling motorcar... The throttle operates beautifully smoothly, and the engine responds beautifully to it at all ties... Once warm the M1 asks to be driven hard for hours on end...Perhaps the car's greatest joy is being able to consistently use its huge reserves of power to rocket out of corners and past others."

Only ever intended as a limited-edition model, the M1 ceased production after a little over 450 examples had been built, just exceeding the minimum of 400 required for Group 4 homologation, which would have preceded homologation for Group 5. In the event, the abandonment of the Group 5 Silhouette Formula robbed the car of its raison d'Ãªtre, though the one-make Procar BMW M1 Championship series run at Formula 1 Grand Prix races in 1979 and '80 provided BMW Motorsport with a valuable showcase by way of consolation. The series ran for only those two years, Nicki Lauda winning the championship in 1979 and Nelson Piquet in 1980. A new M1 road car was awarded to each winner. Out of the 453 production cars completed, 399 were road going units while the remainder were made for motor sport. 

Delivered new in Germany, this example is finished in red with contrasting black leather and fabric interior. The BMW has belonged to the current vendor since 2010 (the car that previously belonged to the director of one of the most prestigious French fine jewelry houses on Place VendÃ´me). There are invoices dating back to 2010 on file for various works, services and spares parts totaling approximately â¬50,000. At 24,468 kilometres the engine was comprehensively restored (photographs and invoices on file) and the clutch replaced by BMW Service at 30,610 kilometres. The odometer reading at time of cataloguing was 30,615 kilometres. 

An important landmark in BMW's history, and in particular of its involvement with motor sport in the post-war era, the M1 is already highly collectible and is surely destined to become increasingly sought after by discerning aficionados of the marque. Offered with French registration documents, an expert report, photos of the engine restoration, and the aforementioned invoices. This BMW M1 ticks all the boxes: Giugiaro styling, superb and reliable BMW engine, beautiful colour combination, and long-term enthusiastic ownership.

THE HISPANO-SUIZA 16HP RABASSADOR

Hispano-Suiza's Barcelona factory produced a number of distinctive sporting automobiles during the early 1920s, before the marque became more widely associated with the large luxury cars such as the H6 and J12 models of the thirties that would define its reputation in later years. Among the more specialized of these early machines was the 16 HP Rabassada, a shortened-chassis derivative named for the Rabassada Hill Climb in the Serra de Collserola outside Barcelona - an important testing ground for automobiles of the day. The variant reflected Hispano-Suiza's interest in competition and high-performance development, combining a compact chassis with a four-cylinder 3-liter engine. A car of similar specification was developed at the direction of company president DamiÃ¡n Mateu for the 3-liter racing class and tested at the Rabassada Hill Climb event.

THE CAR OFFERED

Chassis 5688 is believed to be the only surviving 16HP Rabassada. Built in Barcelona in 1922, it combines the model's shortened chassis with the 2.9-liter engine, producing a period-rated 60hp at 2,300rpm (16HP denoted the horsepower rating for governmental taxation purposes, based on the size of the engine rather than true horsepower output). This engine and chassis were coupled with lightweight sporting two-seat coachwork, creating a powerful combination that secured its place in competition. Its subsequent history is unusually well established within the Hispano-Suiza collecting community. The car was acquired during the 1960s by Michigan collector William J. Markley, who commissioned its restoration during his ownership. In the late 1980s it passed to Terence E. Adderley, remaining in his collection for more than three decades.

The car continues to display evidence of that earlier restoration, including factory stampings on the engine and the serial-number plate mounted on the dashboard. Such details provide tangible links to its Barcelona origins while also reflecting the care with which the automobile has been maintained through its long-term collector ownership.

With its uncommon Rabassada specification, compact proportions, sporting bodywork and direct connection to Hispano-Suiza's early competition ambitions, chassis 5688 offers a different perspective on a marque better known for its grander automobiles. Its exceptional rarity, documented collector history and identifying details make it a particularly engaging example of the sporting Hispano-Suizas produced in Barcelona during the company's formative years.

"When it was first announced by Mercedes-Benz, the production 300 SL CoupÃ© was a startling car built to the German concern's customarily startling standards, but above all what left the general public most open-mouthed about the new car was its upward-opening Gullwing doors...!" - Motors, 1963.

Post-war, Mercedes-Benz had returned to competition in 1952, fielding two of its new 300 SL (W194) sports cars in the Mille Miglia. The pair finishing a creditable 2nd and 4th overall in this most difficult of events, and this promising start was followed up by a win in the challenging Carrera Panamericana. The works first raced the 300 SL (Sport Leicht) in open form, but for the Le Mans 24-Hour Race in June a trio of 'gullwing'-doored coupÃ©s was entered. High sills were a feature of the multi-tubular spaceframe chassis, and while access was not a problem of the open car, the enclosed coupÃ© bodywork required innovative thinking - hence the gullwing doors. Karl Kling and Hans Klenk duly brought their 'Silver Arrow' home in 1st place at Le Mans and the 300 SL was on its way to becoming part of motor sporting legend.

Its development encouraged by the influential United States Mercedes-Benz importer, Max Hoffman, the production 300 SL was unveiled at the International Motor Sports Show in New York in February 1954. The production 300 SL road car retained the spaceframe chassis and lightweight aluminium-alloy bodywork of the W194 racer, while its mechanical underpinnings, like the latter's, owed much to the contemporary Mercedes-Benz 300 luxury saloon. A 2,996cc overhead-camshaft inline six, the 300 SL's engine was canted over at 45 degrees to achieve a low bonnet line and produced 215bhp (DIN) at 5,800rpm using Bosch mechanical fuel injection; it was the first time such an induction system had been used on a production automobile. A four-speed, all-synchromesh manual gearbox transmitted power to the hypoid bevel rear axle. Suspension was independent all round: by wishbones and coil springs at the front, with swing axles and coil springs at the rear.

A production 300 SL (W198) was tested by Road & Track magazine in 1955, accelerating from 0-60mph in 7.4 seconds on its way to a top speed of 140mph (225km/h), a quite extraordinary performance at the time. Half expecting the long-awaited 300 SL to provide an anti-climax, R&T were delighted to find the new car, "far beyond our wildest expectations. In fact, we can state unequivocally that in our opinion the 300 SL coupÃ© is the ultimate in an all-round sportscar. It combines more desirable features in one streamlined package than we ever imagined or hoped would be possible. Performance? It accelerates from a dead start to 100mph in just over 17 seconds. Dual purpose? A production model 300 SL can make a very acceptable showing in any type of sportscar competition. Yet the car is extremely tractable and easy to drive in traffic. Comfort? The fully enclosed 300 SL is the most comfortable (and safe) high-speed 'cross-country' car built today".

A 300 SL roadster featuring conventional doors was first exhibited at the Geneva Salon in May 1957, and although built in greater numbers has never matched the immortal Gullwing for desirability. Its racing parentage notwithstanding, the 300 SL remains a thoroughly practical car, as civilised in city traffic as it is exhilarating on the Autostrada. By the time 300 SL Gullwing CoupÃ© production ceased in 1957, some 1,400 examples had found customers. 

Few post-war sports cars have achieved the legendary status of the Mercedes-Benz 300 SL, and today the model is both rare and highly sought after by connoisseurs of fine automobiles.

According to its associated history, this 1955 Mercedes-Benz 300 SL CoupÃ© was delivered new to Spain that same year. One of only three Gullwings exported new to Spain, it was exported to Venezuela in the 1970s and then moved to the USA, where a comprehensive restoration was carried out during the 1980s. During that restoration, the car was fitted with a 1957-model engine; its present colour scheme of solid grey with red leather upholstery being adopted at the same time. 

In the 1990s the Mercedes returned to Europe where it remained in the ownership of a German collector for 19 years. In 2012 ownership passed to a German collector then in 2016 to a Austrian collector. The current Luxemburg-based collector has owned the car since 2023. That same year, the Gullwing underwent another comprehensive, documented restoration, including extensive work to the body. The associated documentation is available to the successful purchaser. The car's specification, including its later (1957) engine, should be considered in conjunction with the available documentation. As well as the aforementioned restoration records, the car comes with a copy of the 2012 German Fahrzeugbrief (registration document) and an Austrian expertise carried out in May 2016. Additional documentation consists of a FIVA Identity Card and Luxembourg registration documents. 

Belonging to a Luxemburg collector since 2023, the car represents an attractive opportunity to acquire one of Mercedes-Benz's most iconic sports cars, combining the unmistakable styling and advanced engineering of the original Gullwing with a documented restoration history. Its rarity, enduring visual appeal and place in the history of Mercedes-Benz make the 300 SL Gullwing CoupÃ© an important addition to any serious collection of significant post-war sports cars.

It is the stuff of legend that Ferrari-owning industrialist Ferruccio Lamborghini only turned to automobile manufacture as a result of receiving off-hand treatment at Maranello, vowing to build a better car. A successful manufacturer of tractors and related machinery, Lamborghini possessed the resources to realise his dream without having to compromise. Lamborghini's first production car, the Touring-styled 350GT, debuted at the 1964 Geneva Motor Show. The work of two of Italy's most illustrious automobile designers, the 350GT featured a glorious 3.5-litre, four-cam V12 designed by Giotto Bizzarrini, housed in a chassis penned by Gianpaolo Dallara. The 350GT's four camshafts and all-independent suspension meant that it upstaged the best that Ferrari offered at the time, but to compete with his Maranello rival's larger models, Lamborghini needed a four-seater, and the 400GT 2+2 duly appeared in 1966. 

A development of the 350GT, the newcomer used an enlarged - to 3,929cc - V12. This 4.0-litre unit had first appeared in 1965, finding its way into a handful of late 350GTs, this interim model being known as the 400GT. The latter's claimed maximum power was 320bhp - up from the 350GT's 270 - an output sufficient to make the former a 150mph-plus (240km/h-plus) car. The 400GT 2+2 retained the overall, and highly acclaimed, looks of the 350GT while contriving to be slightly taller in the interests of increased rear-passenger headroom. Bodies were now steel (the 350GT's had been aluminium) and the 400GT 2+2 had the twin headlights that had already been adopted in place of the oval originals, largely to meet the USA's requirements. Despite its novice status as an automobile manufacturer, Lamborghini soon dispelled any lingering doubts about its ability to compete with the world's best Grand Tourers. 

Reviewing the 400GT in its 2+2 form in 1967, Autocar magazine voted it "better than all the equivalent exotic and home-bred machinery in this glamorous corner of the fast-car market". The relaxed manner of its long-legged performance was reckoned the finest quality of the Lamborghini, its V12 engine being judged to have the broadest range of smooth torque the testers had experienced. Autocar concluded: "To achieve this level of performance without noise, fuss, temperament or drama is an achievement; in the time taken for development, it is nothing short of sensational." One of only 247 units built between 1966 and 1968, this matching-numbers, 'time-warp' Lamborghini 400GT 2+2 was invoiced on 20th September 1967 by the factory in Sant'Agata Bolognese to the Swiss Lamborghini importer, Garage Foitek AG of Zurich. 

The total cost as noted on the invoice (copy on file) was 5,000,000 Italian Lire (to be paid in cash!) while the original colour combination is recorded as Azzuro Fiat (light metallic blue) with tobacco leather interior. The original-equipment tyres were Pirelli, while the windscreen had a blue band across the top. Other fitted options were air conditioning and a radio. Garage Foitek in turn invoiced the car to its first owner, a resident of Zurich, on 22nd September 1967, for the price of CHF 53,000 less a discount of CHF 9,000 (copy invoice on file). He did not keep the car for long as he had ordered a brand-new Espada; indeed, Foitek had already sold the 400GT (on 26th June 1968) to the second owner, with the provision that he would let the first owner use the car in the month of August '68. The price recorded for the now used Lamborghini was CHF 37,000 (invoice on file). 

The second owner, a well-known Swiss industrialist, obviously enjoyed the car tremendously, as he kept it for the rest of his life, clocking up just under 87,000 kilometres on the believed-correct odometer. As the Lamborghini has always been meticulously looked after, it has never needed a restoration and is presented today in what can only be described as remarkably original 'time-warp' condition. The Lamborghini's late owner was no stranger to sports and racing cars, as he won the Swiss Amateur Championship in a BMW 328 in 1937 in the sports car class, racing at Maloya, Montreux Caux, Klausen and Rheineck Walzenhausen, among others. He held the track record for the mountain race at Rheineck Waldhausen, which remained unbroken for many years after the war.

A serial owner of high end sports cars, he met the Swiss Lamborghini importer Karl Foitek at the Geneva Motor Show; deciding between an Aston Martin DB6 and this Lamborghini 400GT 2+2, he opted for the latter and the car would remain for more than 50 years in the family. An engineer and entrepreneur himself, he felt more attracted by the Lamborghini and admired Ferruccio Lamborghini's ability to produce such high-end sports cars within a short time frame, and which, in his opinion, were more advanced, more powerful and at the same time more reliable than the longer established competition of Ferrari and Maserati. The car's V12 engine was very flexible, and in combination with the all-synchro five-speed gearbox and easy to operate re-circulating ball steering, made light work of the Swiss roads and mountain passes. The car was first serviced by Garage Foitek AG and then by Garage Speich AG in Zurich while in his custody. Importantly, the car has always been registered and in use throughout.

In 2022 the car passed on to its third owner, a true classic car connoisseur. The car was first entrusted to Traber of Toffen in Switzerland for a first big service and checkup as well as the fitment of Avon tires (invoice for CHF 5,445 on file).

A weak spot were the lower parts of the doors as they showed some corrosion. Their rectification was entrusted to none other than RenÃ© GroÎ²e Restaurierungen in Wusterwitz in Germany. They carefully removed the aluminium door skins from the frames, de-rusted and repaired the frames and colour-matched the original Nitro paint (most of the car is believed to still have the original nitro paint), as the objective was to preserve the originality of the car as a whole. At the same time the seat base of the driver's seat was carefully dismantled and new seat webbing fitted whilst the original leather has been preserved. An invoice of more than â¬ 28,500 is on file. More recently this elegant Lamborghini was sent to Italy to a well-known Lamborghini expert for some mechanical work which included an overhaul of the clutch, adjustment of the gear lever mechanism, refurbishing the slave cylinder, the fixing of some minor oil leaks, fitting of new spark plugs and adjusting the carburettors. These stunning Gran Turismo Lamborghinis rarely come to the market, and there can be few, if any, more desirable than this beautiful, un-restored example, which exudes the most charming patina. As we often say, they are only original once... This 400GT 2+2 is ready to be enjoyed by next owner, only its fourth in over 50 years, and comes with copies of the aforementioned original invoices, original owner's manual (in Italian), original warranty card and original Declaration of Conformity (signed by Lamborghini), recent invoices as well as German Historic registration documents as well as a current German TÃV (roadworthiness certificate).

"It is a thrill to drive a car like the Dino, one whose capabilities are far beyond what even an expert driver can use in most real-world motoring, and that is the Dino's reason for being. The real joy of a good mid-engined car is in its handling and braking and the Dino shone as we expected it to. The steering is quick without being super quick, and it transmits by what seems a carefully planned amount of feedback exactly what is going on at the tyres. Thanks to the layout's low polar moment of inertia the car responds instantly to it. The Dino's cornering limits are very high... " â Road & Track. 

It was the need for a production-based engine for the new Formula 2 that had prompted the introduction of a 'junior' Ferrari, the Dino 206 GT, at the Turin Motor Show in 1967. The latest in a line of Dino V6 'quad-cam' engines stretching back to the late 1950s, the new unit proved as successful on the racetrack as in the showroom, Derek Bell and Ernesto Brambilla both winning races in the European Championship, while Andrea de Adamich triumphed in the 1968 Argentine Temporada series. 

Building on experienced gained with its successful limited edition Dino 206S sports-racer of 1966, Ferrari retained the racer's mid-engined layout for the road car but installed the power unit transversely rather than longitudinally. A compact, aluminium-bodied coupÃ© of striking appearance, the Pininfarina-styled Dino - named after Enzo Ferrari's late son Alfredino Ferrari and intended as the first of a separate but related marque - was powered by a 2.0-litre, four-cam V6 driving via an in-unit five-speed transaxle. The motor's 180 brake horsepower was good enough to propel the lightweight, aerodynamically-efficient Dino to 142mph, and while there were few complaints about the car's performance, the high cost enforced by its aluminium construction hindered sales. 

A 2.4-litre version on a longer wheelbase - the 246 GT - replaced the original Dino 206 in late 1969. Built by Scaglietti, the body was now steel and the cylinder block cast-iron. Produced for little more than a year and in limited numbers, the Dino 206 GT is widely regarded as the connoisseur's Dino. Total production amounted to only 152 coupÃ©s, all to European specification, between chassis numbers '00102 to '00410'. Key features unique to the 206 GT include the following: 

â¢ All-aluminium bodywork
â¢ Shorter wheelbase, enhancing agility and turn-in
â¢ 2.0-litre all-alloy V6, 180 bhp
â¢ Rudge knock-off wheels with straight-eared spinners
â¢ Thin bumpers and lighter exterior trim
â¢ External fuel filler cap
â¢ Six engine-lid louvres per side (seven on the 246)
â¢ Girling brake calipers 
â¢ Painted aluminium dashboard panel
â¢ Black-painted cam covers
â¢ Unique gear lever knob with resin-embedded shift pattern
â¢ Firewall-mounted headrests
â¢ Passenger footrest/grab handle
â¢ Centre-console climate controls
â¢ Wood-rim steering wheel 

Early interior trim details, including distinctive vinyl grain and cloth seat inserts with Terry-style texture, further differentiate this 206 GT from later production. Notably, early cars carried minimal Ferrari branding, reflecting the Dino's original positioning as a marque in its own right. The only visible Ferrari marking was often limited to the air-filter cover plate. 

Based on factory records, registry correspondence, period documentation and surviving materials, the history of this Dino 206 GT is known and documented. The 28th Dino 206 GT produced, chassis number '00150' was delivered new in Italy in November 1968 to Dino Ravasio & Figli in Verona, finished in its original and highly desirable colour combination of Rosso Chiaro Ferrari (20-R-190) with Nero (161) leather interior and Panno Rosso (red cloth) seat inserts. This specification is confirmed by registry correspondence and aligns with the car as presented today (with the exception of the red cloth seat inserts). This car's engine and gearbox carry matching serial numbers. 

This car was originally registered in Rome in 1968 and retains its Italian black number plates, 'Roma F20552', a rare and evocative feature that significantly enhances its historical presence and authenticity. In 1997 the Dino was purchased by a Roman. Correspondence with Dino historian and registry authority Matthias Bartz confirms that by 2005 the car was owned by another Italian. While a complete uninterrupted ownership chain has not been established, all known custodians appear to have been knowledgeable enthusiasts, with no inconsistencies within the documented timeline. 

In 2016 the car was acquired by the current Belgian owner, under whose custodianship it has been carefully preserved and responsibly maintained, with a clear emphasis on maintaining originality and mechanical correctness. The Dino is accompanied by extensive documentation including the following: 

â¢ Uso e Manutenzione (owner's handbook)
â¢ Ferrari Classiche letter dated 2016 with original factory specifications (signed by Michel Rayneri)
â¢ Dino expert correspondence confirming delivery details and original specification
â¢ Italian libretto (copy dated 15/10/1997)
â¢ Matching-number identification photographs of engine and gearbox
â¢ Invoices and records for recent works carried out 

The car benefits from documented professional maintenance, including a recent and comprehensive major service, ensuring it is mechanically sorted while remaining original. An invoice on file details a thorough mechanical overhaul performed during the winter of 2023, including: 

â¢ Comprehensive engine service with replacement of all fluids
â¢ Removal, overhaul, and reinstallation of Weber carburettors
â¢ Cooling system overhaul, including water pump and thermostat replacement
â¢ Brake system overhaul, with front and rear caliper rebuild and replacement of flexible and rigid brake lines
â¢ Fuel system service, including tank cleaning and replacement of hoses
â¢ Suspension inspection, with replacement of bearings and joints where required
â¢ Clutch cable replacement
â¢ Radiator and oil cooler servicing
â¢ Extensive parts renewal and 38 hours of specialist labour

This work ensures the Dino is mechanically correct, properly sorted and ready for use, without compromising its originality or period character.

This Dino 206 GT is a high-quality and authentic example. The aluminium bodywork displays correct panel definition, while the mechanical components reflect careful, informed ownership rather than cosmetic over-restoration. The interior trim retains correct production details.

With a mere 152 examples produced, the Dino 206 GT is rarer than most contemporary Ferrari V12 road cars and significantly rarer than the later 246 GT.

As the market increasingly appreciates the Dino family of Ferraris, the 206 GT has emerged as the ultimate connoisseur's Dino. Correctly specified, Italian-delivered examples with matching numbers, original details and credible documentation - all characteristics of this example - are now firmly established among the most desirable of all Ferraris. 

This car, the 28th Dino ever produced, with its original specification, Italian black plates, documented history, and comprehensive recent mechanical works, represents an exceptional opportunity to acquire one of the most historically important and emotionally rewarding Ferraris ever produced.

Introduced in 1985, the Ferrari 328 GTB was similar to the preceding 308 GTB apart from its 3.2-litre engine. Representing the second generation of Ferrari's V8-engined road cars, the entirely new 308 GTB had debuted at the Paris Salon in 1975. This particular model line had begun in 1973 with the Bertone-styled and Dino-badged 308 GT4 2+2 four-seater, and the latter's amidships-mounted, double-overhead-camshaft 3.0-litre V8 was used in dry-sump form for the 308 GTB.

Built on a shorter wheelbase, the 308 GTB marked a welcome return to Pininfarina styling and was manufactured by Scaglietti. Further developments included the introduction in 1977 of an open GTS version with Targa-style removable roof; the adoption of Bosch K-Jetronic fuel injection (1980); and, finally, cylinder heads with four valves per cylinder (1982). 

In 1985, the 308 was superseded by the mechanically similar but larger engined 328 GTB. By increasing both bore and stroke, the quattrovalvole engine's capacity was raised to 3,186cc which, together with other improvements, lifted maximum power to 270bhp. Top speed was raised to 263km/h with the sprint to 100km/h covered in a fraction over 6.4 seconds. Externally, the elegant simplicity of Pininfarina's original 308 had been diluted somewhat by the addition of Testarossa-style moulded bumpers, deeper rear valance, and an unobtrusive roof spoiler.

AMG, which is now the official performance division of Mercedes-Benz, has a long history of producing high-performance derivatives of Mercedes' standard production vehicles, and these improved versions enjoy an enthusiastic following world-wide, with prominent figures of the motorsports, entertainment, sport, and business communities being counted among aficionados. 

With the introduction of the Mercedes-Benz SLS AMG in 2010, the Affalterbach-based firm took a significant step forward. First seen at the 2009 Frankfurt Motor Show and acknowledged as a tribute to the legendary 300 SL 'Gullwing' coupÃ© of the 1950s â arguably the world's first supercar â the Mercedes-Benz SLS AMG was notable as the first car to be designed in-house by AMG. A collectors' item from the day it was announced, the newcomer featured 'Gullwing' doors like its illustrious predecessor and succeeded the Mercedes-Benz SLR McLaren at the top of the German manufacturer's range. Styled by Mercedes-Benz's Mark Fetherston, the SLS AMG received numerous prestigious design awards, and is the only automobile ever to have won the (gold) Design Award of the Federal Republic of Germany. An open roadster version was introduced for 2011.

Boasting a chassis/body of mainly aluminium construction, the SLS (Sport Leicht Super) was powered by a 6.2-litre V8 engine producing 563bhp initially - the most powerful normally aspirated production car engine of its day - while the seven-speed dual-clutch automatic transmission was similarly state-of-the-art. A rear wing, extendable at high speeds, kept the SLS stable at its near-200mph maximum, while its low weight (3,573lbs) helped the car lap the Mercedes-Benz test track quicker than its SLR McLaren predecessor. 

Not surprisingly, given its pedigree, the SLS AMG proved very popular with racing drivers, Formula 1 World Champion Lewis Hamilton among them, while the list of celebrity owners includes Eddie Murphy, Arnold Schwarzenegger, Al Pacino, Roger Federer, Sylvester Stallone, and Tom Hanks.  Coachwork by FLM Panelcraft

There had been 'estate' or 'shooting brake' conversions of Aston Martins in the past, most notably the 12 DB5s built by coachbuilder Harold Radford, who would go on to build a further seven on the DB6 platform; this example, however, is the work of London-based FLM Panelcraft. By all accounts FLM's was a more practical design, boasting a higher roof line, split folding tailgate, and opening side windows.

The culmination of Aston-Martin's long-running line of 'DB' six-cylinder sports saloons, the DB6 was introduced in 1965 at the London Motor Show. Although recognisably related to the Touring-styled DB4 of 1958, the DB6 abandoned the Superleggera body structure of its predecessors in favour of a conventional steel fabrication. The wheelbase was now 4" longer than before, resulting in an extensive restyle with more-raked windscreen, raised roofline and re-shaped rear quarter windows. Opening front quarter lights made a re-appearance, but the major change was at the rear where a Kamm-style tail with spoiler improved the aerodynamics, greatly enhancing stability at high speeds. 

"The tail lip halves the aerodynamic lift around maximum speed and brings in its train greater headroom and more luggage space," revealed Motor magazine, concluding that the DB6 was one of the finest sports cars it had tested. "The DB6 with its longer wheelbase and better headroom makes an Aston Martin available to the far wider four-seater market, and the design is in every way superior to the previous model. A purist might have though that the longer wheelbase would affect the near-perfect balance of the DB5, but if anything the DB6 is better."

The Tadek Marek-designed six-cylinder engine had been enlarged to 3,995cc for the preceding DB5, and remained unchanged. Power output on triple SU carburettors was 282bhp, rising to 325bhp in Vantage specification. Borg-Warner automatic transmission was offered alongside the standard ZF five-speed gearbox, and for the first time there was optional power-assisted steering. Introduced in July 1969, the DB6 Mk2 incorporated many components shared with the new DBS, most obviously the latter's wider wheels that necessitated flaring the front and rear wheelarches. All Mk2 Vantages came with the highest (325bhp) 'C' state of tune, while all cars benefited from power-assisted steering as standard. Production lasted until November 1970, during which time 240 DB6 Mk2s were manufactured, only 71 of which were to Vantage specification while fewer than half of these had the five-speed manual gearbox.

Last-of-the-line models are always sought after by discerning collectors, and few are more highly prized that the final flowering of the glorious 'David Brown' six-cylinder series, considered by many to be the last of the 'real' Aston Martins. 

FLM Panelcraft's conversion greatly appealed to the late Innes Ireland, one of motor sport's most charismatic characters. An ex-Team Lotus Formula 1 driver and many-time Le Mans competitor, Innes was intimately involved with Aston Martin throughout the firm's racing heyday and assisted with the development of the DB6. He bought the first of the three FLM Panelcraft shooting brakes produced. 

The sole example completed on a left-hand drive chassis, this car, 'DB6/2366/L', was ordered by a Mr Farrish of Texas, USA finished in Pacific Blue with a Beige Connolly leather interior. The car left the factory equipped with Normalair air conditioning; chrome wheels with three-ear hub caps; a heated rear screen; engine breather valve system; Fiamm horns; and a limited slip differential. However, it would appear that Mr Farrish soon lost interest in the project. After passing through the hands of various owners, the DB6 resurfaced in partly dismantled condition in the Netherlands.

Purchased by a French collector, '2366/L' was subject to a bare-metal restoration in the UK over fifteen-month period by renowned marque specialists Spray Tec of Wellingborough. In April 1990 the DB6 was advertised for sale in Auto Passion magazine. At that time it was finished in British Racing Green, but by July 1990, when it appeared in the short-lived Auto Live magazine, had been refinished in the light green livery it has today.

Successfully displayed at several concours events, including Goodwood, Parc de Bagatelle and Schwetzingen, 'DB6/2366/L' was acquired by a prominent European private collection in September 2006. A relatively recent acquisition by our vendor, this ultra-rare Aston Martin is offered with concours awards, an owner's guide, some pictures of the restoration, a copy of the Aston Martin build sheet, a copy of an older French registration documents as well as Belgian registration papers. Finally, you can take your dog out in style!

Despite numerous racetrack successes that included Juan Manuel Fangio's fifth World Championship - at the wheel of a 250F - and runner-up spot in the World Sports Car Championship with the fabulous 450S - both in 1957 - Maserati was by that time facing a bleak future. Its parent company's financial difficulties forced a withdrawal from racing, and Maserati's survival strategy for the 1960s centred on establishing the company as a producer of road cars.

The Modena marque's new era began in 1957 with the launch of the 3500 GT, its first road car built in significant numbers. A luxury 2+2 featuring beautiful Superleggera aluminium coachwork by Touring, the 3500 GT drew heavily on Maserati's competition experience, employing a tubular chassis frame and an engine derived from the 350S sports car unit of 1956. 

The 3500 GT's designer was none other than Giulio Alfieri, creator of the immortal Tipo 60/61 'Birdcage' sports-racer and the man responsible for developing the 250F into a World Championship winner. The twin-overhead-camshaft, six-cylinder engine was a close relative of that used in the 250F and developed around 220bhp initially, later examples producing 235bhp on Lucas mechanical fuel injection. Built initially with drum brakes and four-speed transmission, the 3500 GT was progressively updated, gaining five speeds, front disc brakes and, finally, all-disc braking. 

A car possessing such impeccable antecedents not unnaturally attracted the attention of Italy's finest carrozzerie: Allemano, Bertone and Frua all created bodies for the 3500 GT chassis. Most coupÃ©s were the work of Touring, while all but one (a Frua-bodied example) of the much less common Spyder version were the work of Vignale. 

The example offered here represents the pinnacle of the model's development, being delivered with the five-speed ZF gearbox, disc brakes all round. Rare original options include a limited-slip differential, while the Lucas injection has been replaced with a more easily maintained triple Weber carburettor setup. A 2024 expertise report describes the car as in 'very good condition'.

The Jaguar XJ-S was introduced in 1975 as the successor to the celebrated E-Type. Conceived as a sophisticated high-speed grand tourer, it combined Jaguar's smooth and powerful V12 engine with long-distance refinement and unmistakable British elegance. During the early 1990s, the XJ-S provided the basis for one of the most ambitious and exclusive Jaguar conversions of the period.

The XJ-S Monaco was created by engineer and designer Paul Bailey, whose Bristol-based company, PBB Design, developed a dramatically restyled interpretation of Jaguar's V12 Grand Tourer. Bailey had gained experience in the engineering and specialist-vehicle industry, including work on bespoke Range Rover and Rolls-Royce projects, before establishing PBB Design in 1987.

The Monaco was conceived as a much more sporting and imposing XJ-S, with extensively redesigned coachwork, wider bodywork, distinctive front and rear styling, bespoke wheels and exceptionally wide tyres. The development process involved the creation of a full-scale model, allowing Bailey to refine the proportions and the way light fell across the car's sculpted surfaces. The finished design was sufficiently distinctive to stand apart from the standard Jaguar while retaining the fundamental refinement and effortless performance of the XJ-S.

Depending on the customers' requirements, PBB Design could also incorporate significant mechanical upgrades. These included enhanced braking systems, revised suspension, upgraded engine management, and larger-capacity V12 engines. Some cars were fitted with engines prepared by AJ6 Engineering, while individual specifications could vary considerably from one example to another.

Production was undertaken in extremely limited numbers. Contemporary and later sources generally refer to a total of approximately 11 cars, including both coupÃ©s and convertibles, built by 2001 when the project folded, although the exact number remains the subject of discussion. The Monaco therefore ranks among the rarest and most unusual interpretations of the Jaguar XJ-S.

This 1993 Jaguar XJ-S V12 Convertible, chassis number 'SAJJNAFS4ER190061', is understood to be one of the very few Monaco conversions produced by PBB Design and may be the final example completed. The car is reported to have been built in 1993 and has remained in the hands of the same Belgian collector since 2018. 

This Monaco Convertible combines the imposing wide-body styling of the PBB design with the effortless performance of Jaguar's V12-powered open Grand Tourer. Its distinctive appearance, bespoke detailing and rarity make it immediately recognisable, while the electrically operated convertible hood - which closes perfectly and lowers quickly with a simple press of a button - adds an additional degree of exclusivity and enjoyment.

This Monaco's specification is understood to include a 6.0-litre V12 engine prepared by AJ6 Engineering, developing approximately 380bhp, together with upgraded Jaguar Sport ventilated disc brakes and a four-speed automatic transmission. These details should be read in conjunction with the accompanying documentation, as PBB Design built its cars to individual customer requirements and specifications.

Retained by the Belgian collector for many years, this exceptionally rare PBB Design Monaco represents a fascinating opportunity to acquire a highly individual piece of British automotive design history. With its status as possibly the final Monaco produced, limited production, distinctive styling and long-term ownership, it is a car of considerable interest to collectors of unusual coachbuilt and specialist Jaguars.

Created to spearhead Mercedes-Benz's return to competition in the post-war era, the 300 SL debuted in the 1952 Mille Miglia, finishing 2nd and 4th overall. Wins in the Carrera Pan-Americana and at Le Mans followed, and the 300 SL was on its way to becoming part of motor sporting legend. Max Hoffman, the Mercedes-Benz importer for North America, believed there would be a market for a road-going version and managed to convince the factory that such a car would be a success. 

The first racers were open topped but before the '52 season's end the distinctive 'Gullwing' doored CoupÃ© had appeared. Unusually high sills were a feature of the multi-tubular spaceframe chassis, and while access was not a problem of the open car, the adoption of coupÃ© bodywork required innovative thinking - hence the Gullwing doors. 

Launched in 1954, the production 300 SL retained the spaceframe chassis of the racer and was powered by a 2,996cc, overhead-camshaft, inline six canted at 45 degrees to achieve a lower, more aerodynamic bonnet line. Using Bosch's innovative direct fuel injection, this state-of-the-art power unit produced 215bhp at 5,800rpm. A four-speed gearbox transmitted power to the hypoid bevel rear axle, while suspension was independent all round by wishbones and coil springs at the front with swing axles and coil springs at the rear. 

Tested by the highly respected American magazine Road & Track in 1955, the 300 SL accelerated from 0-60mph in 7.4 seconds, going on to achieve a top speed of 140mph: outstanding figures for its day. It was, arguably, the world's first supercar. Its racing parentage notwithstanding, the 300 SL was and remains a thoroughly practical automobile, as civilised in city driving as it is exhilarating on the highway. 

Clearly the 300 SL CoupÃ© would be a hard act to follow, yet the Roadster version, introduced just three years later, succeeded in bettering its closed cousin's already exemplary road manners. Built with conventional doors, the 300 SL Roadster was first exhibited at the Geneva Salon in May 1957 and was an immediate hit with the 1950s 'Jet Set' of royalty, actors and socialites. The production of an open 300 SL involved altering the cockpit area, where the spaceframe was redesigned to permit lower sills for improved access. At the same time the rear suspension was changed to incorporate low-pivot swing axles. Disc brakes were standardised from March 1961, while towards the end of production a small batch of Roadsters was completed with an aluminium cylinder block. 

The Roadster's neutral steering characteristics received fulsome praise from Road & Track. A 0-60mph time of 7.0 seconds and a top speed of 130mph (209km/h) were recorded, making the 300 SL Roadster one of the fastest convertibles of its day. The 300 SL Roadster sold well for a car that cost more than a Ferrari 250 GT California Spyder, and would outlive the 300 SL CoupÃ©, which ceased production in 1957, by several years. Roadster production ceased in 1963 after 1,858 cars had been built, some 70% being exported to the USA, and today the model is both rare and highly sought after.

According to the Datenkarte (copy on file), this stunning 300 SL Roadster was completed at the factory on 26th July 1961 and delivered new in Germany. The original colour was white (colour code 050) with tan leather interior (colour code 040), the same as today, Further options include a radio (code 511), automatic aerial (531), whitewall tyres (641), sport seats (401), among others. Most importantly, being a 1961 model, it has the most desirable combination of factory-fitted disc brakes and the less capricious iron-block engine, so arguably has the best specification for a 300 SL Roadster. 

On 25th June 1973 the engine was replaced by Mercedes-Benz themselves at their official Hamburg branch. The odometer reading at the time was 66,569 kilometres and the replacement engine number ended in '002938', only five numbers higher than the original one which ended in '002933'. The change is documented in the accompanying Mercedes-Benz service book which was issued by Mercedes-Benz for that purpose. Importantly, the replacement engine is of the iron-block type, same as the original. 

The car has been subjected to a meticulous frame-off restoration by the highly respected German 300 SL specialist Lars Rombelsheim of LARO Sportwagen. The result is simply stunning, and expertise reports issued by an official German appraiser in 2012 and 2017 respectively rate the car as condition '1', the highest (the range goes from 1 â 6). The appraiser specifically mentioned the frame-off, bare-metal restoration to original specification, and the accompanying documentation as deciding factors for the appraisal. This documentation includes copies of the previous German registration document; copies of the original Datenkarte with all the important part numbers recorded; and the Mercedes Service Book recording that the engine had been exchanged by Mercedes-Benz themselves. The car also comes with current German registration documents. The aforementioned expertise report is very thorough and worthy of the closest inspection. 

The current custodian purchased the Mercedes, already restored, in 2017. The preceding owner had bought the car in 2005, and the associated Kraftfahrzeugbrief lists only one previous owner, who most likely was a well-known Porsche racing driver and successful building contractor. As far as we know this is effectively a three-owner car from new, adding to its pedigree. 

This 300 SL Roadster certainly ticks all the boxes: specification, provenance, documentation and meticulous restoration by one of the foremost experts for this model.

Last of the classic six-cylinder Maseratis, the Pietro Frua-styled Mistral built on the success of the first-of-the-line 3500GT of 1957. Maserati's survival strategy for the 1960s had centred on establishing the company - which hitherto had mainly concentrated on its Grand Prix and sports car racing activities - as a producer of road cars. The Modena marque's new era began in 1957 with the launch at the Geneva Salon of the Touring-bodied 3500GT. A luxury '2+2', the 3500GT drew heavily on Maserati's competition experience, employing a tubular chassis frame and an engine derived from the 350S sports car unit of 1956. Suspension was independent at the front by wishbones and coil springs, while at the back there was a conventional live axle/semi-elliptic arrangement. 

The 3500GT's designer was none other than Giulio Alfieri, creator of the immortal Tipo 60/61 'Birdcage' sports-racer and the man responsible for developing the 250F into a World Championship winner. The twin-overhead-camshaft, six-cylinder engine was a close relative of that used in the 250F and developed around 220bhp initially, later examples producing 235bhp on Lucas mechanical fuel injection. Built initially with drum brakes and four-speed transmission, the 3500GT was progressively updated, gaining five speeds, front disc brakes and, finally, all-disc braking. 
The next development of the theme arrived in 1962. Built on the short-wheelbase chassis of the Vignale-bodied 3500GT spider, the Sebring coupÃ© featured a five-speed gearbox, disc brakes, and fuel injection as standard equipment, with automatic transmission, air conditioning and a limited-slip differential available as options. 

The marque's final iteration, the Mistral, commenced production in 1963. The 3.7-litre version of the famous long-stroke engine was fitted to most cars, other options being the 3.5-litre or, from 1966, the 4.0-litre unit, all of which came with Lucas fuel injection. A handsome two-seater on a shortened, square-tube chassis, the Mistral was built in coupÃ© and spider versions, the former's opening rear window hatch making it unusually practical for a sports car. A five-speed gearbox, disc brakes and fuel injection were standard equipment; automatic transmission, air conditioning, and a limited-slip differential the options. Production ceased in 1970, by which time 827 coupÃ©s and 123 spiders had been built. 

According to the build sheet from Maserati, this Mistral was built in November 1966 and delivered in the most attractive colour combination of Celeste Chiaro (light-blue metallic) with a black leather interior. It was delivered via the Genoa-based concessionaire Automar SrL to its first owner in the same city. The car later found its way to the United States (a Missouri title from 1990 is on file) before being repatriated to Italy in 2005 via Germany. Since 2024 it has been with our vendor, a committed Maserati fan, sharing its garage with a Maserati Quattroporte. 

This Mistral is an older restoration which still presents nicely. The interior has at some point been changed from black to very elegant tan leather, while the exterior colour is still the original and most elegant Celeste Chiaro. The Mistral also retains its original engine. The car is offered with German Historic (H) registration documents; Maserati Classiche documentation including a Certificate of Origin, Technical and Aesthetic Characteristics Certificate, and Historical Information Certificate; a copy of an older ASI certificate; an old US title; a copy of an older Italian libretto; an owner's manual in Italian; and a Classic Data report.

"While the Gallardo and MurciÃ©lago can be credited for revitalising Lamborghini for the 21st century, the HuracÃ¡n felt like another big step into modernity when it arrived in 2014. On paper it ticked every box as a junior supercar to rival the likes of Ferrari's 458 and the McLaren 650S: over 600bhp from Lambo's signature V10, four-wheel drive, a dual-clutch gearbox (finally) and a totally fresh design and interior." - evo magazine. 

The HuracÃ¡n (Spanish for Hurricane) made its official debut at the 2014 Geneva Auto Show, with deliveries commencing later that year. Its chassis was an entirely new design in - mostly - aluminium, featuring a central tunnel and rear bulkhead in carbon fibre for increased stiffness. Powering the newcomer was a development of the 5.2-litre V10 shared with the outgoing Gallardo, which delivered its 610PS to the road via a seven-speed, dual clutch, electronically controlled, four-wheel drive transmission system. The compact coupÃ© bodywork was typically Lamborghini, boasting its manufacturer's customary combination of smooth curves and sharp edges. This low-drag shape enabled the HuracÃ¡n to breach the all-important 320 km/h benchmark, albeit by only 4 kilometres per hour, with the 0-97km/h (0-60mph) dash accomplished in a mere 2.5 seconds. Retardation was handled by carbon discs all round. 

The interior was notable as the first use by Lamborghini of parent-company Audi's 12.3" TFT 'virtual cockpit' and featured the customary heated/adjustable seating and leather/Alcantara upholstery. Other notable features include full LED headlamps, power steering, and an ANIMA (Adaptive Network Intelligent Management) driving modes selector controlling the engine, transmission, suspension, brakes, etc. The HuracÃ¡n also met the demanding EU6 emissions targets. 

Introduced in 2015 as the convertible counterpart to the celebrated HuracÃ¡n coupÃ©, the Spyder retained the formidable capabilities of its fixed-roof sibling while offering the additional sensory pleasure of open-top driving. The electrically operated fabric roof can be raised or lowered in approximately 17 seconds at speeds of up to 50 km/h, allowing the driver better to enjoy the unmistakable soundtrack of that glorious V10 engine. 1971 De Tomaso Mangusta CoupÃ©

One of the very first supercars, the Mangusta effectively established De Tomaso as a serious automobile manufacturer and a worthy rival for Ferrari, Lamborghini and Maserati. Originally a constructor of racing cars, De Tomaso did not build its first road car - the Vallelunga - until 1965. A pretty, mid-engined coupÃ© powered by a 1.5-litre Ford four-cylinder engine, the Vallelunga was built in small numbers and was not a success, but did contribute its short-wheelbase, backbone chassis - albeit extensively re-engineered - to the Mangusta.

Introduced in 1967, the Mangusta (mongoose) was powered by a mid-mounted 289ci (4.7-litre) Ford V8 engine. Also used to power Ford's GT40 Le Mans challenger, the iconic '289' produced 306bhp as installed in the Mangusta, which also used the GT40's early-type ZF transaxle. Later Mangusta production used the Ford 302ci (5.0-litre) engine together with a later-type ZF transmission. Carrozzeria Ghia's Giorgetto Giugiaro contributed the striking coachwork featuring 'gull wing' engine covers, which had been intended for Giotto Bizzarrini. There is much in Giugiaro's design that echoes his work when designing the Maserati Ghibli, Iso Grifo, Ferrari 250 Berlinetta Bertone and, of course, the timeless Alfa Romeo Giulia Sprint GT. With 300-or-so horsepower on tap in its original form, the aerodynamic Mangusta was good for a top speed in the region of 155mph. All-round disc brakes helped restrain this outstanding performance. 

De Tomaso enjoyed close links with the Ford Motor Company at that time and the American firm helped put the Mangusta into larger scale production than would otherwise have been possible. Nevertheless, only 401 examples were made between 1967 and 1972 compared with 765 examples of the contemporary Lamborghini Miura, and any Mangusta is extremely rare. The three marque registries estimate that there are only some 250 Mangustas remaining worldwide. 

This particular example - chassis number '8MA1200' â was built to European specification with four fixed headlights (not the USA's retractable headlamps) and as such is the most sought-after by collectors. Beautifully restored and extensively documented, it is recognised within the international De Tomaso community as one of the finest in existence. This car's interior features its original leather seats, dashboard, steering wheel, gear knob, etc in addition to power windows, full instrumentation and the original radio. 

Chassis number '8MA1200' was produced on 28th February 1971 and sold new in Italy, registered in Rome as 'P49701-Roma'. In the early 2000s the Mangusta underwent a ground-upwards restoration in Canada by Wingho Auto Classique (Montreal). The restoration was widely praised within the De Tomaso community.

On 10th August 2005 the car was offered for sale in QuÃ©bec, Canada. At that time, it was described as a 'Best in Show Concours Winner' and 'one of the finest Mangustas available'. At some time between 2007 and 2010 the car was exported to Europe, and in 2010 was offered for sale in the Netherlands, recently imported from Canada. In 2011 the Mangusta was seen at various European classic events and was offered for sale at Techno-Classica Essen. In 2012 the car was sold via Anamera and in 2016 was offered by Thiesen Automobiles, Germany. In January 2018 the car was acquired by a Brussels-based collector. This car has been followed, discussed, and admired publicly for over two decades, with consistent recognition of its quality. The body is straight and beautifully presented.

Holding up extremely well, the early-2000s restoration was comprehensive and executed to a very high standard. A small number of modifications were made for enhanced reliability and usability:
â¢ Jack-shaft removed, compact alternator fitted
â¢ Electronic ignition fitted
â¢ Rear lamps added (first as fog lamps, later converted to reversing lights for European regulations)
â¢ Rear suspension cross-member modification for added rigidity

These documented changes are well-known and accepted within the De Tomaso community. 

A reference-quality De Tomaso Mangusta, '8MA1200' represents the perfect synthesis of Italian design and American muscle, preserved through a exacting restoration and decades of knowledgeable ownership. One of the most compelling and beautiful mid-engined GT cars of the late 1960s, and a cornerstone piece for any serious collector.

Publicly displayed for the first time at the Frankfurt Auto Show in 1967, Mercedes-Benz's fifteen 'New Generation' models went on sale the following January. But although the fuel-injected 280 SE saloon shared its bodyshell with the 'New Generation' 280 S, the 280 SE CoupÃ© and Convertible retained the elegant looks of the outgoing 250 SE that had debuted back in 1959 on the 220 SE, designed by Paul Bracq. The 2,778cc overhead-camshaft six-cylinder Type M130 engine, though, was all new. In fuel-injected 'SE' form the seven-bearing M130 produced 160bhp at 5,500rpm, an output sufficient to propel the manual transmission model to 118mph with the automatic, an increasingly popular choice, not far behind. Just as important in an age when automobile induced atmospheric pollution was becoming a hot political issue, was the fact that the M130 brought with it improved fuel economy and more efficient emissions control. 

The suspension was essentially the same as that of the equivalent saloon model, albeit reconfigured for a lower ride height, with braking courtesy of discs all round. Plush and well appointed, the interiors featured a leather-covered dashboard; (usually) leather upholstery; a Becker radio; and round speedometer and rev counter flanking vertically stacked gauges. The thickly padded convertible top was manually operated, while air conditioning, electric windows, central locking and power assisted steering were among the several options listed. Production of the 280 SE CoupÃ© and Convertible totalled a little over 5,000 units between 1968 and 1972 when production ceased, and today these timelessly elegant Grand Tourers are keenly sought after by connoisseurs of fine automobiles. It is worthwhile noting that the 280 SE Cabriolet is the next most desirable variant after the now prohibitively expensive 280 SE 3.5 Cabriolet.

In 2012, the official Mercedes-Benz dealer in Monaco sold the car to the current owner, who imported and registered it in Belgium (purchase invoice on file).

One of Mercedes-Benz's most elegant open cars of the period, the W111 Cabriolet combines superb coachwork with refined performance and comfort for which the brand is renowned.

Some of the frontal panels were shared with the standard four-door saloon but otherwise the new bodyshells were unique, featuring a distinctive dipping upper wing line with parallel crease, and a revised, more rounded posterior. Rightly regarded as one of the all-time great classic sports cars, Cobra succeeded in capturing the hearts of enthusiasts like few of its contemporaries. Only 1,000-or-so Cobras of all types were built between 1962 and 1967. 

Convinced that a market existed for an inexpensive sports car combining European chassis engineering and American V8 power, Le Mans-winning Texan racing driver Carroll Shelby concocted an unlikely alliance between AC Cars and the Ford Motor Company. The former's Ace provided the simple twin-tube chassis frame - designed by John Tojeiro - into which was persuaded one of Ford's lightweight, small-block V8s. To cope with the projected power increase, the Ace chassis was strengthened with heavier gauge tubing and supplied fitted with four-wheel disc brakes. Barely any heavier than an Ace fitted with a Bristol engine yet endowed with double the power and torque, the Cobra turned in a breathtaking performance, racing to 60mph in 4.4 seconds and reaching speeds of 100mph in under 12, exceptional figures by early 1960s standards and none too shabby even today.

The 260ci (4.2-litre) prototype first ran in January 1962, with production commencing later that year. Exclusively for the USA initially, Cobras - minus engines - were sent from England to be finished off by Shelby in California, and it was not until late in 1963 that AC Cars in Thames Ditton got around to building the first fully finished cars to European specification. 

After 75 Cobras had been built with the 260ci engine, the more powerful 289ci (4.7-litre) unit was standardised in 1963. Rack-and-pinion steering was the major MkII update; then in 1965 a new, stronger, coil-suspended MkIII chassis was introduced to accommodate Ford's 427ci (7.0-litre) V8. Wider bodywork, extended wheelarch flares and a bigger radiator intake combined to create the definitive Cobra MkIII look. 

Chassis number 'COB6047''was built by AC cars in right-hand drive configuration and originally finished in Vineyard Green with a beige interior. The Cobra was despatched to the H R Owen dealership in Kensington, West London and on 7th July 1965 was sold to its first owner, one J A 'Derry' MacPherson; the car was registered as 'EYT 78C' , a London mark. 

The Cobra did not remain in England for very long, MacPherson taking it with him to San Jose, California, and in the summer of 1966 it was driven by him to the USA's East Coast. According to the Cobra Register: "The electric fan quit halfway across the country, and MacPherson visited his uncle's shop, the Pine Plains Garage (Pine Plains, NY) for repairs. He later repeated the trip in west-bound mode." Concerned that the appreciative crowds that the Cobra never failed to attract would damage the lightweight alloy bodywork, MacPherson eventually traded 'COB6047' against a Porsche 914. 

In the early 1970s the Cobra was acquired by Mike Math of Venice, California, passing to another owner, in Texas, in the 1980s. Subsequently the car was purchased by Lynn Detzel of Oklahoma, who repainted it red. It was Detzel, or possibly a subsequent owner, who converted the Cobra from right- to left-hand drive. Circa 1984, 'COB6047' was acquired by George Raterink of Colorado. Eaterink added a white stripe to the red livery before selling it to another Colorado resident, Harry Matthews. According to the Cobra Register: "Matthews went through the car, making various repairs as well as detailing and fine-tuning the vehicle."

In 1987, Matthews sold 'COB6047' via Steve Mier's Encore Motorcars of Lakewood, Colorado to its next private owner: Rick Cole of California. Its next owner, Bill Schenck of Arcadia, California, acquired the Cobra from Cole later in 1987. Schenck kept 'COB6047' until 2011 when the car was sold to a new owner in France via Grand Prix Classics of La Jolla, California. The Cobra is currently registered in France. 

As presented today, 'COB6047' has been the subject of a comprehensive restoration both mechanically and cosmetically, and was featured and tested by Mustang & Shelby Magazine for their edition number '025'. The car comes with its jack, spare wheel, tonneau cover and other items. Accompanying documentation consists of a history file; Cobra Register extract; invoices file; US title; UK registration document; French registration papers; and a valid technical inspection.

With a mere 1,000-or-so made by AC Cars and Shelby, early Cobras are offered for sale only rarely and 'COB6047' represents a wonderful opportunity to acquire a fine example of this classic and highly sought-after Anglo-American sports car.

Ferrari's flagship model, the Testarossa supercar revived a famous name from the Italian company's past when it arrived in 1984. A 'next generation' 512 Berlinetta Boxer, the Testarossa retained its predecessor's amidships-mounted, 5.0-litre, flat-12 engine. Reflecting Ferrari's racing heritage, the latter had first appeared in 4.4-litre form in the 365 GT4 BB having been developed using experience gained from the Maranello firm's World Championship-winning, flat-12 Formula 1 and sports-racing units. As deployed in the Testarossa, this unique engine now boasted a maximum power output raised to 380bhp at 6,300rpm courtesy of four-valve cylinder heads. Despite the power increase, smoothness and drivability were enhanced, making for excellent top gear flexibility and a maximum speed of 290km/h (180mph). 

Rivalling Lamborghini's Countach for presence, the Pininfarina-styled Testarossa succeeded brilliantly, the gill slats feeding air to its side-mounted radiators being one of the modern era's most instantly recognisable â and copied - styling devices. A larger car than the 512 BB - the increase in width being necessary to accommodate wider tyres - the Testarossa managed the trick of combining high downforce with a low coefficient of drag, its graceful body being notable for the absence of extraneous spoilers and other such devices. Despite the increase in size over the 512 BB, the Testarossa was lighter than its predecessor, the body - its steel doors and roof excepted - being, somewhat unusually for a production Ferrari, of aluminium. Luxury touches in the well-equipped cabin included air conditioning, electrically adjustable seats, tilting steering wheel and plentiful leather. Unlike some of its rivals, the Testarossa possessed light controls and was relatively easy to drive, factors which, allied to its outstanding performance and stunning looks, contributed to an instant and sustained high level of demand.

Ferruccio Lamborghini's first production car, the Touring-styled 350 GT, was launched at the 1964 Geneva Motor Show featuring a glorious four-cam 3.5-litre V12 engine by Giotto Bizzarrini, which was housed in a chassis the work of Giampaolo Dallara. The line of front-engined Grand Tourers continued with the 4.0-litre 400 GT and Islero 2+2s, the Espada four-seater saloon and finally, in 1970, the Jarama, destined to be the last of Lamborghini's front-engined sports cars. By this time Giampaolo Dallara - co-designer of the legendary Lamborghini Miura alongside Paolo Stanzani - had left Sant'Agata, so the task of developing the new car fell to Stanzani. 

Launched at the 1970 Geneva Motor Show and named after a region of Spain famous for its fighting bulls, this new 240km/h-plus four-seater abandoned Lamborghini's original spaceframe chassis in favour of a platform-type unitary construction, based on the Espada's but of significantly shorter wheelbase. An unusual styling feature was the nose with its quadruple headlamps partially obscured by electrically raised covers. The Jarama was styled at Carrozzeria Bertone by Marcello Gandini, the man responsible for the sublime looks of the Miura, but with body panels built in steel by Bertone and assembled by Marazzi. An improved 'S' version, with 365bhp V12 engine, appeared in 1972 boasting a much-improved cockpit, while later developments included Torqueflite automatic transmission and power-assisted steering. The Jarama continued in production until 1976, by which time 327 cars had been built, 150 of them to 'S' specification.
