"For a man who wants the last word in sports cars, a mid-engined machine is essential. Racing single-seaters are built to this configuration and so the mid-engined car must be right! 

"It is thus of great interest that the famous Maserati firm, which has tended to be somewhat conservative in recent years, has now placed an advanced mid-engined coupÃ© on the market." â John Bolster, Autosport. 

The highlight of the 1971 Geneva Salon was undoubtedly the sensational new Maserati Bora. With the Bora's introduction, the great Modenese manufacturer followed other supercar constructors in going mid-engined while at the same time abandoning its traditional tubular chassis technology in favour of unitary construction. Named after an Adriatic wind, the Bora was the work of Giorgetto Giugiaro's Ital Design, at least as far as its bodyshell was concerned; the mid-mounted engine was Maserati's familiar four-cam V8 in 4.7-litre form, the five-speed transaxle came from ZF and the all-independent double-wishbone suspension was penned by Giulio Alfieri, co-designer of the legendary 250F Formula 1 Grand Prix car. One of the first 'new generation' models to appear following Maserati's acquisition by CitroÃ«n, the Bora used the latter's hydraulic technology to adjust seats and pedals, raise the headlamps, and operate the excellent power-assisted brakes. A slippery shape plus 310bhp made for a very fast car - top speed was over 160mph (258km/h) - and the Bora had acceleration, handling and braking to match. The subsequent 4.9-litre version was even faster. 

By January 1976, Maserati's management apparently had discussed shelving the Bora but later that year decided to continue. Only some 25 Boras were made that year, and the total produced was 564, the 4.7/4.9-litre split being 289/235. The type was finally phased out in 1979. 

Motor magazine concluded its March 1973 Road test thus: "The Bora impressed us as one of the best and most civilized mid-engined exotics we've tried, better developed than most of its ilk and immensely rewarding to drive, especially to drive fast on cross-country roads." What more could any enthusiast want? The Bora was a stunning supercar by any standards, both then and now.

"Over many decades one has come to expect so much of a Lancia that one judges it inevitably by very high standards.

Representing the highest level in current Italian concept and workmanship, the Flaminia coupÃ© has a strong and attractive character, underlined by impeccable road manners, which make it as rewarding to drive in this country (the UK) as in its native land." - Autocar, 1960.

The coupÃ© and convertible versions of the Lancia Flaminia were made in relatively small numbers and surviving examples in good condition are, therefore, quite rare. Lancia's Pinin Farina-styled Flaminia saloon had debuted at the 1956 Turin Motor Show. Designed by newly recruited Antonio Fessia and intended as a replacement for the Aurelia, the Flaminia retained its predecessor's mechanical layout, though the form of unitary construction was changed and Lancia's traditional 'sliding pillar' independent front suspension, which had been used on every model since 1922, gave way to a more modern double wishbone and coil spring arrangement. Aurelia carry-overs were the overhead-valve, 60-degree V6 engine and De Dion rear transaxle (with inboard brakes). The former had been extensively reworked by Fessia, resulting in a much stronger power unit than that designed by his legendary predecessor, Vittorio Jano.

The short-wheelbase Flaminia coupÃ© appeared in 1958, followed by the Touring-styled GT and GTL (2+2) coupÃ©s and the convertible. The latter trio shared a further shortened (to 99") wheelbase with the Sport and Super Sport models, and all featured disc brakes and increased power. The 2,458cc V6 produced 119bhp when installed in the more sporting Flaminias, with 140bhp available in the triple-carburettor '3C' models from 1961, which was further increased when the 2,775cc version arrived in 1963. Parts availability for these classic Lancias is excellent, with the UK's Omicron Engineering holding plentiful stocks. There are also marque specialists in Italy, Holland, and the USA, as well as an enthusiastic owners' club. These cars cost as much as an Aston Martin DB4 when new and were arguably much better engineered.

Beautifully finished in silver with a black leather interior, this Flaminia CoupÃ© was purchased for the vendor's private collection in 2018; he then had the engine overhauled and a new clutch fitted. More expensive than the 300 SL sports car and almost double the price of the contemporary top-of-the-range Cadillac, the Mercedes-Benz 300 S was one of the world's most exclusive automobiles. It is also historically significant as one of Mercedes-Benz's first all-new designs of the post-war era, debuting at the Frankfurt Auto Show in 1951. The 300's arrival re-established Mercedes-Benz in the front rank of prestige car manufacturers, marking as it did a return to the marque's tradition of building high-performance luxury automobiles of the finest quality.

"To the characteristics of high performance, impressive appearance and fine detail finish which distinguished the big Mercedes models of pre-war days are added new virtues of silence, flexibility and lightness of control, while the latest rear suspension, a product of long experience on Grand Prix cars and touring cars, confers a degree of security at high speeds on rough and slippery surfaces which it would be very difficult indeed to equal," observed Autocar magazine.

Custom built by Mercedes-Benz's most experienced craftsmen, the Mercedes-Benz 300 was luxuriously appointed and trimmed with materials of the highest quality. Fast and elegant, it was one of very few contemporary vehicles capable of carrying six passengers in comfort at sustained high speeds. The 300 was the car of choice among West German government officials, and throughout Europe and the USA was widely favoured by businessmen, financiers and politicians. Indeed, 'Adenauer' became the 300's unofficial model name, after German Chancellor Konrad Adenauer, its most famous customer.

Undeniably beautiful, the 300 S models looked exactly what they were: well built, well engineered and well designed. Mercedes was, arguably, far ahead of the curve with their offerings of hard-to-improve-upon coachwork in the pre-war era. As the 1950s began they were even clearer in their tailoring of cars and appropriate bodies for their discerning clientele. 

The conservatively styled 300 Saloon was soon joined by the 300 S (Super), a model that succeeded in recapturing all the elegance of the pre-war 540K. Introduced at the Paris Salon in October 1951, the 300 S was built in two-seater coupÃ©, cabriolet and roadster forms on a shortened 300 saloon chassis.

Not only was the two-seater 300 S considerably lighter than the saloon, it was also more powerful, boasting an engine equipped with triple (as opposed to twin) Solex carburettors and a raised compression ratio. Maximum power output was increased to 150bhp and top speed to 110mph (176km/h). Unlike some of its spartanly furnished contemporaries, the 300 S boasted a lavishly equipped interior featuring supple leather upholstery; beautiful burr walnut trim, chromium-plated dashboard instrumentation and precision-made switchgear.

As one might expect of Mercedes, they have kept comprehensive archival records of their production and were pleased to confirm for Bonhams that this 300 S Roadster was delivered new on 2nd April 1953. Its destination was the USA and the new Roadster was finished in Cream (DB 629) and upholstered in red-brown leather. The Datenkarte confirms that it is matching numbers (engine and chassis) and was delivered new via Riviera Motors in San Francisco, California. 

Between 2003 and 2010 the Mercedes was restored for the Samsung Car Collection at a cost of more than â¬ 415,000 (invoices on file). Sold by Bonhams at our Mercedes-Benz Museum Sale in Stuttgart in 2016, and purchased by the current owner via a well-respected classic Mercedes-Benz dealer in 2017, it has always been well looked after. Used sparingly since the rebuild's completion, it still presents beautifully as only the best restorations do. The quality of the work is absolutely breathtaking, and the attention to detail and factory correctness is equally impressive. Particularly worthy of note is the rare floor-mounted gear lever, a sportier option than the much more common steering column-mounted gear change. 

This spectacular car is offered with a substantial file containing the German registration documents; restoration invoices; copies of the Datenkarte; and a lubrication and maintenance service booklet.

Delivered new in Germany, this 991.2-era Porsche 911 Turbo S 'GTStreet R' is an imposing and highly modified example of the marque's supremely capable modern performance coupÃ©. The car has covered 38,615 kilometres from new and has been enhanced with a raft of desirable TechArt performance and cosmetic upgrades. 

This particular Porsche 911 Turbo S has been transformed by the lauded tuning company TechArt into its blisteringly fast 'GTStreet R' specification. The car is finished in Crayon exterior colour with a matte-black GTStreet R racing stripe and side decals together with red highlights and matte carbon-fibre trim elements. Inside, the cabin features black leather upholstery with contrasting white belts/stitching and Alcantara accents, punctuated by carbon-fibre trim. 

The car now rides on an aftermarket set of 20" centre-lock TechArt 'Formula IV Race' forged alloy wheels, shod with Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 tyres. Inboard of the wheels we find orange TechArt-branded brake callipers gripping carbon-ceramic discs. 

The generous factory specification includes headlamp washers; front and rear parking sensors with reversing camera; LED headlights; multifunctional heated steering wheel; electric panoramic glass sunroof; switchable driving modes; wireless charging; keyless entry; Sport Chrono package; automatic start/stop function; electrically adjustable dampers; dual-zone automatic air conditioning; and a touchscreen PCM infotainment system with satellite navigation, Apple CarPlay, and Bluetooth connectivity. 

Externally, this 911 now features a TechArt carbon-fibre body kit, including a front splitter; bonnet; side sills; rear diffuser; wider GT3 RS-style vented wheel arches; extended side air vents; a rear engine lid scoop; and a double-decker rear spoiler. Inside, the cabin has been upgraded with Porsche sport seats; retrimmed steering wheel with the TechArt logo; and a numbered GTStreet R plaque (this car is number '30' of 87 built). 

Under the rear lid sits a remapped 3.8-litre twin-turbocharged flat-six, now producing up to 581bhp and 678lb/ft of torque, driving all four wheels via a seven-speed PDK dual-clutch transmission with paddle shift. The engine benefits from new aftermarket turbochargers; a remap; and a new quad-exit TechArt exhaust system. 

The paintwork is reported to be in excellent condition given the car's age, though the seller notes small blemishes on the front of the car. Inside, save for light signs of use, the cabin presents very well. The seller is not aware of any mechanical or electrical faults. The car is offered with Belgian registration papers; its service booklet (stamped on three occasions); and all its instruction manuals. The service booklet was last stamped on 18th August 2024 at 22,502 kilometres (current odometer reading is 38,615 kilometres). 

Summing up: this 991.2-era Porsche 911 Turbo S 'GTStreet R' is a striking example of the marque's eminently capable all-season performance car, transformed with a raft of desirable TechArt performance and cosmetic upgrades. Presented in impressive condition throughout, with an imposing black and orange colour scheme complementing its widened stance, and boasting blistering pace courtesy of its upgraded 3.8-litre twin-turbocharged flat-six, it would make a distinctive addition to any collection of high-performance cars, an exhilarating weekend toy, potent daily driver, or formidable track-day weapon.

BMW's emergence as a manufacturer of fine sporting motor cars can be traced back to the annual Eifelrennen event held at the NÃ¼rburgring on 14th June 1936, when Ernst Henne beat a field that included 1Â½-litre monoposto racing cars driving the prototype of what would become one of the most iconic sports cars of all time: the legendary '328'. The fact that this overwhelming victory had been achieved only eight years after BMW's establishment as an automobile manufacturer is all the more remarkable. 

Lacking the resources of larger and longer established rivals, BMW had adopted an evolutionary, 'mix and match' approach to model development. Thus the 328 employed the tubular chassis, transverse-leaf independent front suspension and live rear axle of the 319; the cylinder block and hydraulic brakes of the 326; and a body incorporating stylistic elements of the 319/1 Sport and 329. With the 328, BMW's Chief Engineer Fritz Fiedler turned the conventional chassis design on its head, coming up with a frame that combined lightness and stiffness in equal measure - virtues that permitted the use of relatively soft springing with all its attendant advantages. In short: the 328 was the first truly modern sports car.

The 328's 1,971cc six-cylinder engine featured an ingenious new cylinder head, designed by Rudolf Schleicher, which incorporated hemispherical combustion chambers and inclined valves without recourse to overhead camshafts. Instead, the Type 326 engine's single, block-mounted camshaft and pushrod valve actuation were retained, thus avoiding an expensive redesign. Two rocker shafts were employed, one situated above each bank of valves, giving the engine an external appearance almost indistinguishable from that of a twin-overhead-cam design. Down-draught inlet ports contributed to the motor's deep breathing, and its tune-ability made it a popular choice for British racing car constructors, most notably Cooper, during the 1950s. The 328 engine produced 80bhp, an exemplary output for a normally aspirated 2.0-litre unit at that time, with more available in race trim. 

The two door-less prototypes and the first batch of cars were lightweight racers with aluminium coachwork and were intended to establish the 328's competition credentials before production proper got underway. Available from the late summer of 1936, the production 328s featured doors and a convertible hood, and were well equipped and very comfortable in the manner of the best Grandes RoutiÃ¨res. On the racetrack the 328 reigned supreme, winning its class at the Mille Miglia, Le Mans, Spa 24 Hours, and Britain's Tourist Trophy. In 1940 an example fitted with special aerodynamic bodywork won the Mille Miglia outright. 

The most advanced sports car of its day, the 328 remained competitive for years after WW2, a state of affairs that only served to further enhance its reputation, which was out of all proportion to the limited number produced. Between 1936 and 1939 only 464 BMW 328s were made, of which some 300 are estimated to exist today. 

A beautiful example of the legendary BMW 328, this car carries elegant cabriolet coachwork by Wendler and is believed to be one of only 10 such models ever built. An older restoration, the BMW is harmoniously finished in two-tone light green over dark green with a dark green leather interior and features rear wheel spats and a beige hood. The colour combination is most likely original, as depicted by a period black-and-white photograph showing the same contrasts.

Offered with German Historic registration documents, the car formed part of a collection in Denmark before being purchased for a large collection in Germany in 1999.

Generally regarded as one of the very few pre-war models that drives like a post-war car, the legendary BMW 328 is eligible for all the most important Historic events including the Mille Miglia, NÃ¼rburgring Oldtimer GP, and Le Mans Classic.

Few silhouettes in the automotive world carry the weight of history quite like the Mercedes-Benz G-Class. Introduced as long ago as 1979, the Mercedes-Benz G-Class 'GelÃ¤ndewagen' (cross-country vehicle) was the result of a joint venture with Steyr-Daimler-Puch of Austria, a firm with considerable experience in developing four-wheel-drive systems for off-road vehicles. Its purposeful appearance â fundamentally unchanged throughout its life â and engineering excellence has secured the G-Wagen cult status and earned it a reputation as one of the most coveted of classic 4x4s. 

Conceived as a rugged military vehicle, the original 460-series G-Wagen entered civilian life in 1979 and, within a year, had found its way into service as the Vatican's Popemobile. For 1991 an extensively revised (W463) chassis was introduced, incorporating the very latest in off-road traction technology in the form of three electronically engaged differentials in addition to anti-lock brakes. The W463 moved the G-Class from spartan and utilitarian to a luxury model able to compete with the rival Range Rover without softening the character that had made the G-Class a legend in the first place. By 1994 it carried the G-Class name officially, and over the decades since, it has evolved from military workhorse to one of the most coveted status symbols in the world - a shape virtually unchanged across more than four decades, even as the engineering beneath it reached ever further into the extraordinary.

One of the final models released, the G 63 was powered by AMG's 5.5-litre twin-turbocharged V8 engine developing 563bhp, which was delivered to the ground via AMG's Speedshift Plus 7G-tronic automatic transmission. Boasting high ground clearance and long-travel suspension, the AMG G 63 offered greater off-road capability than most customers would ever need in an immensely stylish conveyance with not inconsiderable on-the-road presence. Like the entire model series, the G 63 AMG was produced in Graz, primarily in the factory's hand-finishing section. 

Within G-Class history, no lineage is more extreme, or more exclusive, than the 4Ã4Â² family. It began in 2013 with the G 63 AMG 6Ã6, an outlandish six-wheeled military fantasy turned production reality. Two years later came the first G 500 4Ã4Â², inheriting the 6Ã6's portal axles and widened bodywork in a form suited to both road and trail. The final chapter arrived in 2022: an all-new G 63 4Ã4Â², built for the first time around AMG's full 4.0-litre twin-turbocharged V8, boasting 585bhp and 626lb/ft of torque sent through portal axles otherwise reserved for the Unimog. Mercedes-AMG itself described this car, without qualification, as 'the last of its kind'.

The result is a machine that defies easy categorisation. With three locking differentials, a low-range transfer case, and ground clearance exceeding 35cm, the G 63 4Ã4Â² can conquer terrain that would defeat almost any other production vehicle on earth, and then drive home on the motorway with the effortless V8 shove expected of any modern AMG. It is a contradiction that exists nowhere else in the automotive landscape: equal parts Unimog and supercar, built in strictly limited numbers before Mercedes closed the chapter for good.

What sets this car apart, even within so rarefied a lineage, is its exceptional condition. Finished in Opalite White Magno, and showing only 400 kilometres from new, this G 63 4Ã4Â² has barely left the showroom floor. First registered on 3rd July 2025, it is not simply a well-kept example; it is, to all intents and purposes, a time capsule: the final and most powerful expression of a model line Mercedes itself confirmed would never be repeated, preserved in essentially as-new condition. As one would expect, this example is exceptionally well specified and generously optioned, the list of such items running to almost five A4 pages (inspection recommended). 

As production of the 4Ã4Â² comes to a permanent close, examples in this state of preservation will only become scarcer, and more keenly sought after, with each passing year. For the collector seeking not merely a G 63, but the definitive, final word on one of the most audacious vehicles ever put into series production - offered here in practically unused condition - this is an opportunity unlikely to present itself again.

One of the great names in postwar French motor sport, Alpine was the brainchild of Dieppe garagiste's son, Jean Redele, who began in the early 1950s by developing a competition version of the popular little Renault 4CV, which won its class in the Mille Miglia three years running.

In 1963 Alpine launched the famous A110 Berlinette that became the mainspring of production, its rearward weight bias giving it outstanding cornering characteristics for rallying. In 1969, A110s finished 1-2-3 in the Coupe des Alpes and came 3rdin the Monte Carlo Rally. The following year, Alpines again came 3rd in the Monte and won the Acropolis and Tour de Corse rallies. Alpine driver Jean-Claude Andruet became European Rally Champion.

The Alpine 1600 SC was released in 1973 with the A310 rear axle and overlapping double wishbone suspension with two shock absorbers instead of the previous four, the result being an improvement in stability and handling. In addition, the wheels were secured by four bolts and the door handles replaced with simple push-buttons. Also, a rear panel removable from within the interior enabled access to the engine bay. The 1,605cc Renault 12 Gordini engine was mated to a five-speed gearbox. With 127bhp DIN on tap, the compact and aerodynamic little berlinette had a top speed of 215km/h (133mph). Only 481 units were produced between 1973 and 1975.

This Alpine A110 1600S, chassis number '20470', was delivered by Alpine dealer Vermeersch to its first owner, a jeweller from Gosselies, Belgium on 4th July 1975. Its AA101 body, numbered '10463', was manufactured at Dieppe and originally finished in Alpine Blue. Its engine, numbered '001294', is of the 844-30 type and corresponds to the original specification. On 24th April 1986, the Alpine was registered by a collector in Mons, who subsequently sold it to the current owner's father.

Showing approximately 98,000 kilometres on the odometer today, this Alpine is notable for its rare authenticity; it has never suffered the rigours of competition and retains its attractive original Alpine Blue paintwork. Following a service by a marque specialist, the car is offered with a recent Belgian registration certificate and a Belgian roadworthiness inspection valid until May 2031.

The A110 1600 SC/VD is one of the most desirable versions of Alpine's iconic berlinette, and this exceptionally original example represents a particularly appealing opportunity for the collector seeking an unspoiled example.

"The Jaguar XK150 is undeniably one of the world's fastest and safest cars. It is quiet and exceptionally refined mechanically, docile and comfortable. As with most cars, there are a few body details which could be improved, but we do not know of any more outstanding example of value for money." - Autocar. 

A progressive development of the sensational XK120 and XK140, the XK150 retained the same basic chassis, 3.4-litre engine and four-speed Moss transmission of its predecessors but benefited from an entirely new body providing increased interior space and improved visibility courtesy of a one-piece wraparound windscreen. A higher front wing line and broader radiator grille were other obvious differences, but the new model's main talking point was its Dunlop disc brakes; at last the XK had stopping power to match its prodigious straight-line speed. 

Introduced in the spring of 1957, the XK150 was available at first only in fixed and drophead coupÃ© forms, the open roadster version not appearing until the following year. At 190bhp, the engine's maximum power output was identical to that of the XK140, so performance was little changed. 'Special Equipment' and 'S' versions came with 210 and 250bhp respectively. Overdrive and automatic transmission were options.

This left-hand drive XK150 3.4-Litre Fixed Head CoupÃ©, chassis number 'S834063', benefits from documented provenance. According to its Jaguar Heritage Production Trace Certificate - issued in 2014 and confirming matching numbers - the car was originally supplied through Jaguar Cars, New York and first owned by Mr Warren K Weaver. The XK left the Brown's Lane factory finished in Cotswold Blue with dark blue interior trim. 

The Jaguar subsequently returned to Europe where it has been owned by the same Belgian collector since 2018. Its history is supported by the Jaguar documentation, providing confirmation of its original factory specification and delivery details. This example features tasteful cosmetic modifications, further refining the model's beauty.

The Jaguar XK150 represents the final and most sophisticated evolution of Jaguar's celebrated XK sports car, combining the marque's renowned 3.4-litre twin-cam straight-six with elegant styling, improved comfort and impressive performance, making it equally appealing as a collector's car or for enjoyable Grand Touring.

First registered on 22nd April 1970, the car offered here is the very first example of one of the rarest open BMWs ever produced. This BMW 2002 Cabriolet is not merely rare, it is the prototype: the original car that set the pattern for the following production model. Its unique status is confirmed by factory records and Bauer's contemporary documentation, 

The foundation of BMW's post-war resurgence was the Neue Klasse four-door 1500 saloon and its derivatives, and the company capitalised on their success with the launch of a revised two-door range in 1966. Like the earlier cars, the new 1600 (later 1602) featured unitary construction, all-independent suspension and front disc brakes. 

The larger, 1,990cc engine produced 100bhp at 5,500rpm in single-carburettor configuration and 120bhp on twin Webers when installed in the 2002TI. Models available on the 2002 platform comprised a two-door saloon, three-door Touring estate car, and a Cabriolet, the latter with coachwork by BMW's long-term coachbuilding collaborators, Karosserie Baur of Stuttgart. Built in extremely limited numbers (approximately 200 in total), these cars were effectively hand-crafted conversions. An immense commercial success for the German manufacturer, some 349,000 BMW 2002s of all types had been sold by the time production ceased in 1976. 

This Cabriolet prototype is supported by exceptional documentation, including the following:

â¢ Contemporary correspondence from Karrosserie Baur, confirming its status as the first cabriolet
â¢ Written confirmation from BMW Classic (December 2016) identifying chassis '1558366' as the very first BMW 2002 Cabriolet
â¢ Its original Kraftfahrzeugbrief (German registration document), dating from 1970, documenting its ownership from new
â¢ Restoration records 

The Kraftfahrzeugbrief lists four owners who owned the car from 1980 until the commencement of its restoration in 2015, a remarkably long-term custodianship. Between 2015 and 2016, the BMW underwent an uncompromising 'last-nut-and-bolt' restoration by Holucar Oldtimer Restoration, a highly regarded German specialist. The restoration was executed with an emphasis on correctness, quality and long-term preservation. Retaining original components wherever possible, the works carried out included: a complete body restoration; fully renewed paintwork; all chrome trim restored; and a comprehensive retrim (seats, door panels, convertible hood, hood cover). Crucially, the car retains its original dashboard, instrumentation, radio and steering wheel. 

Our vendor purchased the BMW in 2017. Finished in red with black leather interior and matching convertible hood, the car is presented in period-correct specification. It has seen only limited use post-restoration having covered approximately 1,000 kilometres since the rebuild. The current odometer reading is 37,676 kilometres. 

As appreciation of BMW's early coachbuilt models grows, and as historically significant examples disappear into long-term collections, opportunities to acquire a car of this stature are becoming increasingly rare. Representing a milestone in the history of convertible BMWs, this 2002 Cabriolet Prototype is eligible for exhibitions, top-tier concours and marque-focused events, and is worthy of a place in any important private collection. 

In short: it represents a possibly once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to acquire the very first BMW 2002 Cabriolet ever built. Combining unmatched historical importance, exceptional documentation and a world-class restoration, this prototype stands as one of the most significant BMW 2002s in existence.

Styled in-house by Bill Towns, the beautiful DBS was Aston Martin's first all-new model for many years and caused quite a stir on its arrival in 1967, Autocar magazine observing that: "Without the aid of an Italian stylist the Newport Pagnell team came up with something as modern, handsome and Italianate as anything from the Turin coachbuilders at that time."

Although always intended to house the new Tadek Marek-designed V8 engine, the DBS first appeared with the 4.0-litre 'six' of the concurrently produced DB6. This well proven engine was available in standard tune, producing 282bhp or, as a no cost option, to Vantage specification with triple Weber 45DCOE carburettors, special camshafts, and a higher compression ratio, in which form its maximum was raised to 325bhp.

Beneath its shapely exterior the DBS employed a platform-type chassis with independent suspension all round: wishbone and coil-spring at the front, De Dion with Watts linkage at the rear. Larger and more luxuriously appointed than the DB6, the DBS was, inevitably, heavier, though the Vantage version's top speed of 140mph and a standing quarter-mile time of 16.3 seconds were highly respectable figures nonetheless. Assessing the virtues of Aston's new flagship, Autocar judged it superior to the DB6 in many areas, the bigger DBS offering four full-sized seats in addition to transformed handling and roadholding courtesy of the new rear suspension and standardised power steering.

This DBS Vantage was built as a left-hand drive export model and delivered new in Italy where it was enjoyed by various Italian owners as listed in the copy of the car's libretto. No further information is available regarding its history prior to its purchase in 2007 by one of the previous owners.

The Aston was auctioned by Bonhams at its sale in Paris in June 2021 (Lot 236). At that time the car was described as in good overall condition: "It appears to be solid and would benefit from a mechanical overhaul before returning to the road due to a long period in storage." It was then restored at Classic Affairs. The bodywork was stripped back to bare metal and repainted in Olive Green Metallic. Considerable mechanical work was carried out including an engine overhaul, fuel tank removed for epoxy treatment, cooling system cleaned and other works. At the same time the interior was fully retrimmed in leather and the carpets replaced. Accompanying documentation consists of a French registration certificate, an FFVE certificate, an ACI certificate, a copy of the Italian carta di circolazione, invoices and photographs of the restoration.
